video_title: Bitcoin Is About to Explode — The Fed Just Ran Out of Tools
gist: Jordy Visser argues the past two weeks were a macro regime break: a US-BOJ coordinated yen intervention (the first since 1998), 20-year highs in 30-year yields, an unchanged refunding announcement and the weakest six-month aggregate payroll since 2012 ex-COVID together signal the Fed has run out of tools and must reflate, which he thinks pulls capital into gold, silver and eventually Bitcoin. He simultaneously calls the July AI drawdown a completed panic low (new all-time highs by year end, optical names over memory), frames compute scarcity as the dominant 2-3 year investment fact, and says talent flight plus debt issuance should compress Google's multiple.

themes.theme: Yen intervention and the Fed's exhausted toolkit

insights.claim: The US Treasury selling euros to buy yen in coordination with the Bank of Japan is the first such intervention since 1998 and, per Jordy Visser, reads as desperation rather than routine policy because the stated rationale is not clear the way a bailout or rate cut would be.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: A coordinated FX intervention with no clean explanation is a tell that the authorities are defending the long end; watch dollar-yen and 30-year yields as the trigger set for a reflation trade.
insights.quote: the US for the first time since 1998, that same year with LTCM, coordinated with the BOJ to intervene in the yen. And this has all the hallmarks of desperation.

insights.claim: Visser says the bond market, not equities, is the administration's line in the sand: 30-year US yields just made 20-plus year highs while Japan is a large holder of that paper, so the deficit forces policy to cap long rates even as short-term rate cuts are demanded.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Frames every dislocation as tolerable until long rates spike; a back-end yield breakout is the signal that forces intervention or printing.
insights.quote: The bond market has for the last two years been the line in the sand with the administration.

insights.claim: A quarterly refunding announcement with no change was, to Visser, the confirming signal that authorities have no remaining levers and will end up printing to keep long rates from rising.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: If the policy path resolves to reflation, hard assets and duration-insensitive scarcity trades are the expression, not the long end.
insights.quote: Then we get the refunding announcement where there's no change, which basically says game on to me. Meaning there's nothing we can do.

insights.claim: Visser believes the new Fed chair failed his first test by deferring to the market, saying long-term yields were doing the work for him, and that even a Fed that wanted to be hawkish could not be given the labor and deficit backdrop.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Positions for a Fed that is structurally on hold to easing regardless of rhetoric, making hawkish repricing a fade.
insights.quote: everything that we're learning is even if they wanted to be hawkish, they couldn't be.

insights.claim: The US has arrived at the position Japan held in 1998, when shorting JGBs was called the widowmaker: both now carry inflation above target alongside an unmanageable debt load, which Visser uses as the core argument for why Bitcoin matters now.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Recasts the US as a debt-trap sovereign, which is the intellectual bridge from macro policy exhaustion to a monetary-hedge allocation.
insights.quote: When I was in Japan in 1998, Japan was the only debt game in town. Everyone tried to short JGBs. It was called the widowmaker.

themes.theme: Labor market cracks under AI hiring freeze

insights.claim: Aggregate payroll, which combines hours worked, wages and net hiring, is at its weakest six-month rolling level since 2012 outside of COVID, which Visser reads as evidence the economy is running out of policy options rather than running strong.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: A six-month aggregate payroll trough contradicts the strong-labor narrative and argues for front-end easing being underpriced.
insights.quote: we are at the weakest level since 2012 on a six-month rolling basis, except for during CO.

insights.claim: Average hourly earnings growth has slipped to 3.2% year over year, the weakest of the current trend, while the labor participation rate is falling sharply, a combination Visser says removes the case for further tightening.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Falling wages plus shrinking labor supply is disinflationary in the wage channel; it undercuts hawkish economists and supports duration and hard assets.
insights.quote: today's hourly earnings now puts year-over-year at 3.2% easily the weakest of this trend

insights.claim: Markets still price more than one tightening before year end and a 44% chance of a September hike, which Visser treats as a mispricing against the deteriorating labor data.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: A tradable gap between priced hikes and labor reality; upcoming inflation data is the catalyst that resolves it.
insights.quote: there's still a 44% chance of a hike in the September meeting

insights.claim: Visser argues AI is hitting employment through a hiring freeze rather than mass layoffs, and that everyone including himself has underestimated how quickly AI impact arrives once it starts.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: If the labor channel is hiring rather than firing, headline layoff data will lag and understate AI's macro effect; track hiring rates and participation instead.
insights.quote: So, so far this has been a hiring issue. I don't think we're going to see massive layoffs.

themes.theme: Bitcoin's coiled setup and the crypto fundamentals unlock

insights.claim: Gold, silver and platinum are all breaking out while Bitcoin has not, which Visser attributes to the Clarity Act overhang rather than to a broken monetary-hedge thesis, and he bought silver on the Monday after the yen intervention.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Precious metals leading with Bitcoin lagging frames Bitcoin as the catch-up trade if the legislative overhang clears.
insights.quote: gold is breaking out, platinum's breaking out, silver is breaking out. Bitcoin hasn't broken out yet, but that's because the Clarity Act has been this overhang on it.

insights.claim: Bitcoin holding near short-term highs even as Clarity Act passage odds collapsed from roughly 40% to 17% for the year and Strategy sold Bitcoin is, to Visser, a bullish tell about absorbed supply and exhausted bad news.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Price refusing to fall on stacked negative catalysts is the classic setup for an upside break; watch for confirmation rather than waiting for legislation.
insights.quote: in the face of bad news, the Clarity Act going from 50, well, let's say from 40% all the way down to 17 for the for this year. And at the same point that strategy has sold Bitcoin and not only has it kind of hung here, it's getting close to making new kind of short-term highs.

insights.claim: Visser's trigger for a real crypto move is a technical break, specifically Dogecoin clearing its 20-day and 50-day moving averages as evidence retail has re-engaged.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete, checkable entry signal using a retail-sentiment proxy rather than waiting on macro confirmation.
insights.quote: all it's going to take to get the Bitcoin crowd fired up is a technical breaking point

insights.claim: Visser's sequencing thesis is that AI agents are this year's theme and consumer agents are next year's, which means stablecoin transaction volume grows regardless of whether the Clarity Act passes.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Makes stablecoin rails a legislation-independent volume growth story, decoupling the crypto revenue trade from Washington risk.
insights.quote: AI agents are the theme of this year. The theme of next year is consumer agents, which means transactions and volumes using stablecoin. That is going to happen regardless of the Clarity Act.

insights.claim: Hedge funds have stayed out of crypto because they chase momentum in fundamentals as well as price and crypto had no fundamentals to lean on; once agent-driven transaction revenue attaches real math to network effects, Visser expects institutional money to rotate in, helped by AI names hitting risk limits at 20% daily moves.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific mechanism (fundamental momentum plus Sharpe/risk-limit constraints in AI names) that could drive an institutional capital rotation from AI equities into crypto.
insights.quote: the biggest negative for crypto that keeps hedge funds uninvolved in it is that they're all momentum, not just in price, but in fundamentals. And the problem with crypto is there aren't there haven't been any fundamentals to lean on.

themes.theme: The July AI drawdown as a completed panic low

insights.claim: Visser calls the AI selloff bottomed and predicts many AI names make new all-time highs by year end, arguing the deleveraging was significant, the bounce has follow-through, and good stocks are again responding to good news.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: An explicit, dated call: any dip is a buy for those holding cash, and failure to make new highs by year end invalidates the thesis.
insights.quote: not only are the lows in for the AI names, by the end of the year, we'll be at new all-time highs for for many of them.

insights.claim: Large-cap AI names traded at 80 to 120 volatility during the drawdown, above the highest volatility Bitcoin has seen in the last decade, and fell violently despite rapidly growing earnings because of a fund blowup rather than fundamentals.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Reframes the selloff as a leverage event, not a fundamental repricing, which is why the recovery can be sharp; also flags that AI equities are now the high-vol asset class relative to Bitcoin.
insights.quote: the AI names are trading at volatility well above even I would say the highest level that Bitcoin has traded at in the last decade.

insights.claim: Within AI, Visser prefers optical names over memory into a Vera Rubin cycle, holds a good-sized Nvidia position on the view that it has traded well and is cheap, and is not adding to Micron.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: A concrete intra-AI rotation: fund the trade out of memory and into optics ahead of an expected earnings catalyst.
insights.quote: The area that I'm probably most focused on at this point is the optical names. And the reason the optical names are such a focus is because Vera Rubin is coming.

insights.claim: Visser explicitly fades Michael Hartnett's bull-bear indicator flashing its biggest sell signal, pointing out the same chart since February preceded only a minor pullback followed by higher prices.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: A named sentiment-model fade; useful as a marker of how crowded the bearish positioning signal has become.
insights.quote: despite Michael Hartnet putting out a report saying bull bear indicator is at the biggest sell indicator, I want people to look at that chart since February of this year. We did get a minor pullback and then we went higher.

themes.theme: Compute scarcity and the physical-AI buildout

insights.claim: Visser argues compute should be treated as a commodity like copper, because whether models are open source or frontier the compute requirement is identical, and demand for intelligence is effectively insatiable.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Converts a technology debate into a supply-demand commodity framework, making compute-adjacent capacity the durable exposure regardless of which lab wins.
insights.quote: If there were if we thought of compute the same way we thought of copper, we'd be very very interested in buying as much compute.

insights.claim: Visser cites Elon Musk on the SpaceX earnings call saying memory demand is growing 200% a year against memory capacity growing 20% a year, and attributes the gap to agents spawning sub-agents that consume compute continuously.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: A 10x demand-supply mismatch in memory is the single hardest number in the episode for sizing the semiconductor and memory shortage trade.
insights.quote: memory demand is growing by 200% a year. Memory capacity is growing by 20% a year.

insights.claim: Visser says public semiconductor and industrial infrastructure builders will capture returns before private physical-AI companies do, because the investable horizon is the next two to three years of compute buildout while private robotics bets signal what happens in years three to ten.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Tells investors where to put capital now versus what to merely monitor, and warns against paying up for far-future TAM narratives.
insights.quote: The next 2 to 3 years are about compute, comput, compute.

insights.claim: Hadrian raised $1.3 billion at roughly an $8 billion valuation for robotics-driven factory-as-a-service across about 3 million square feet, and the participation of JP Morgan's strategic defense initiative and Apollo's first-ever venture investment signals large institutions are treating industrial venture as the new private equity rather than lottery-ticket VC.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Private-credit and PE money entering industrial venture at scale is a structural change in who funds re-industrialization and at what cost of capital.
insights.quote: they raised $1.3 billion dollars at like a almost eight billion dollar valuation. And to me the most interesting part was who participated.

themes.theme: Frontier models, enterprise indemnification and AI-native firms

insights.claim: Visser argues large public companies will not adopt open-source models quickly because bureaucracies need indemnification and someone to blame for hallucinations or errors, which protects Anthropic and OpenAI enterprise revenue.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Legal risk transfer, not model quality, is the moat for frontier labs in enterprise; open-source disruption arrives later than model benchmarks imply.
insights.quote: there is no way that they are going to use open-source models quickly in big enterprises

insights.claim: Visser expects Anthropic and OpenAI revenues to keep growing for the next year to eighteen months driven mainly by enterprise and research, with the labs increasingly aligned with government on problems like curing cancer.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Sets a defined window for frontier-lab revenue momentum, useful for pricing private-market exposure and for timing when the thesis needs re-examination.
insights.quote: I just think anthropic and open AI for the next, let's say, year to year and a half, we're going to continue to see their revenues grow.

insights.claim: Visser sees a growing cohort of one-person, million-dollar-revenue AI-native businesses with no bureaucracy and minimal capital or headcount needs, which he expects to eventually compete against public companies including hyperscalers on margins.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: A long-dated structural short on public-equity growth rates and a long on private/small-business formation; margin compression shows up before revenue loss.
insights.quote: It's unprecedented the lack of need of both capital but also human beings.

themes.theme: Google talent flight and multiple compression

insights.claim: With Jeff Dean gone after 27 years and Demis Hassabis moving into another role, Visser argues Google faces genuine uncertainty about terminal value, and combined with a fresh $25 billion debt issuance that uncertainty should compress its multiple.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: An explicit de-rating case on a mega-cap: rising leverage plus talent-driven uncertainty argues for lower multiples, not just slower growth.
insights.quote: Well, if you don't know, shouldn't the multiple compress on the company, especially if it's in the business where it has lots of debt and you don't know?

insights.claim: Visser frames the split inside big tech as AGI-focused researchers chasing personal legacy versus the company needing consumer revenue to fund capex, and concludes talent will gradually leave, which is bad for public-equity growth rates over the next five years.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: A generalizable screen: mega-caps whose research talent is legacy-motivated face a slow leak of the exact people their multiples depend on.
insights.quote: It's all bad for public equities with inside the next 5 years from a growth rate perspective. It's very very good for entrepreneurs and small businesses.

insights.claim: Visser's positioning rule is to be long the companies receiving cash from the AI capex cycle that are exposed to physical constraints rather than to abundance-prone activities like code, with an explicit 18-month horizon before he starts flagging overbuild on the physical side.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: A concrete allocation rule plus a self-imposed expiry date, giving a checkpoint at which to reassess the physical-AI trade.
insights.quote: I want to be long the companies that are getting the cash from these companies that are not exposed to abundance, meaning code.

themes.theme: Trader versus investor playbook in a faster market

insights.claim: Visser uses 50-day rate of change as his core timing tool: he reduced exposure when his 100-name thematic index was up 50% over 50 days, versus a prior five-year norm that peaked near 20% and reset to around minus 10%, which is exactly where it landed after the drawdown.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: A replicable, mechanical overheating gauge that combines time and price, calibrated with actual prior-cycle thresholds for trimming and re-entering.
insights.quote: my thematic portfolio with a 100 names was up 50% over a 50-day period. So, I reduced it.

insights.claim: Visser's advice splits by mandate: investors should stay in the AI trade and not worry, expecting roughly 15% above the S&P, while traders should be wary of getting over their skis when rate of change gets too high.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Separates the timing question from the exposure question so investors do not trade a thesis they should be holding.
insights.quote: Don't worry about it as an investor. Stay in the trade. Sit there. Be happy that you'll get an extra 15% over the S&P.

insights.claim: Visser has discarded calendar seasonality and long-horizon backtested models because AI compresses market time, citing that the worst full year ever for momentum was less bad than what happened in July alone.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: If factor drawdowns now compress a year of pain into a month, risk models calibrated on 40 years of history will systematically understate tail moves.
insights.quote: I've thrown out all the old models. I just think things are moving way too f fast.

insights.claim: Visser values SpaceX on its compute business alone and treats the space business as a free call option, arguing anything near $100 is attractive after the stock ran from about $135 to over $200, fell to roughly 106-108 on a share unlock, and recovered to about 127-128.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Gives an explicit valuation anchor and entry level for a volatile private-market name by separating the boring cash-generative compute asset from the speculative space TAM.
insights.quote: value the business on the compute and then you get the space for free
